newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian dollar finds rate cut settles nothing.
newsitem.headline: Australian dollar finds rate cut settles nothing.

text.p: The Australian dollar finished firmer on the week but short of key recovery levels reflecting relief a long-feared rate cut had passed but a certain amount of unease the whole speculative circus could start again.

Dealers said support had proved to be robust under US$0.7430 and a general assumption this week's easing in official rates to 5.0 percent was the last of the cycle, suggested there was room for a push past Tuesdsay's US$0.7505 peak.
But weak economic figures had already stirred talk a sixth easing was not impossible and a sudden slide in the Kiwi dollar illustrated what happened to currencies with rate trouble.
By 5.00 pm (0700 GMT) the local dollar had settled back at US$0.7445/50 from an early US$0.7460/65 having nudged up from US$0.433/38 late Thursday.
Dealers said a new trading range was forming with good bids and offers seen either side of US$0.7425 and US$0.7505, following the break from a three-week old US$0.7310/7440 band.

The currency suffered in sympathy with the Kiwi dollar which dived 1/2 cent amid heavy offshore selling, partly attributed to speculation the weakening economy would ultimately force the RBNZ to sanction this market-led policy easing. The Kiwi sank to US$0.6445/50 from US$0.6490/97 late Thursday.

Some of the selling spilled over into the A$, particularly as dealers suspected the risks on rates here were also to the downside despite all the well rehearsed arguments about why this week's cut should be the last of the cycle.
The A$ came out the better of the two and pushed to NZ$1.1527/44 from NZ$1.1480/98. It was also up at 88.52/62 yen from 87.60/70 and at 58.4 in trade weighted terms from 58.3.

So far the general assumption in the market has been that Wednesday's cut in official rates to 5.00 percent was probably the last of the cycle and, as this became clearer, the dollar would find more offshore support.
Unfortunately for A$ bulls recent economic data had not exactly co-operated with this comfortable scenario with both building approvals and retail sales weaker than expected.

And the omens were not promising for next week as private banking data suggested housing finance figures Friday would show a fall in commitments of around 5.0 percent in June on top of a surprise 8.4 percent drop the month before.

Neither were analysts confident July jobs data Thursday will show the recovery in employment so long anticipated. Forecasts favour a rise of around 25,000 which even combined with June's 11,900 gain, would still not make up for May's fall of 40,300.

A weak employment result would get the futures market worked up again. The December 90-day bank bill contract stands at 95.12 implying a rate of 4.88 percent, suggesting the market was not entirely convinced the easing cycle had ended.
But there was a sign offshore demand remained healthy in the successful launch of a global A$ bond by Fannie Mae, the second in as many months.
So great was demand for the debt that the amount was upped to A$1.0 billion from A$750 million and offshore investors needed dollars to pay for it.
